title: 2026-03-31 Redwood Discovery - Orion AI - Latency Benchmark
topics: hosted vs dedicated vs private deployment
summary: Orion AI is evaluating Redwood for a latency-sensitive real-time inference use case. Primary requirements: p95 latency <= 300-400ms for short-turn streaming responses, support for ~30-100 concurrent streams depending on mode, and token/sec throughput targets for longer generation. They want a benchmark plan comparing Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private (VPC) and need security docs for SOC2/KMS/SSO. Next step is a pilot/benchmark run and follow-up with pricing and capacity options.
next_steps: Redwood to send dedicated pricing + burst capacity doc (Liam)
Customer to provide representative prompt set and sample traffic profile (Priya)
Schedule benchmarking pilot (Maya + Dana) for week of 2026-04-06
Share SOC2 and VPC architecture docs (Liam)
Follow-up meeting to review pilot results and sizing (2 weeks after pilot)
action_items: Liam Chen: Send Dedicated pricing sheet and burst capacity options (due: 2026-04-02)
Priya Raman: Share canonical prompt set + 5 sample long-turn conversations (~2k tokens) (due: 2026-04-01)
Maya Singh: Prepare benchmark plan + test scripts (hosted/dedicated/private) and proposed metrics (p95, median, tokens/sec, concurrency) (due: 2026-04-03)
transcript:
Header: 2026-03-31 15:00 PST | Duration: 42m
Attendees: Liam Chen (Redwood AE), Maya Singh (Redwood SE), Carlos Vega (Orion CTO), Priya Raman (Orion ML Eng), Dana Ortiz (Orion Infra Lead)

00:00 Liam Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. Quick roll call?
00:04 Carlos Vega: Hi, Carlos here.
00:05 Priya Raman: Priya.
00:06 Dana Ortiz: Dana on infra.
00:07 Liam Chen: Awesome. Maya, wanna do a 30s intro?
00:09 Maya Singh: Yep, Maya, Redwood SE. I focus on perf and deployment, especially dedicated and private setups. Today we wanna understand your targets so we can map hosted vs dedicated vs private.

00:28 Carlos Vega: High level — Orion's building an interactive summarization + QA product for enterprise docs. It's real-time-ish, users care a lot about latency. Our P95 goal for short responses is around 300ms, ideally under 250ms if feasible. For long-form generations we care more about throughput and tokens/sec.
00:47 Priya Raman: To add, our typical session is streaming token-by-token to the UI. Average response length is ~150 tokens but we have 20% of requests that go 1k-2k tokens. Concurrency — we expect 20-30 concurrent live users for the initial launch and scale to 80-100 at peak.
01:08 Dana Ortiz: Security stuff: we need SSO, SAML, SOC2 docs, KMS integration for keys, and VPC connectivity if we go private. Also retention policies, audit logs.

01:21 Maya Singh: Great. A few clarifying q's: that 300ms P95 — is that for first token or end-to-end completion for the ~150-token case?
01:29 Carlos Vega: That's end-to-end for the short 150-token responses — so we mean total time until the UI receives the last token streamed. First-token latency can be slightly lower but it's the completion P95 that matters.
01:39 Maya Singh: Understood. And concurrency numbers — 20-30 steady, 80-100 burst. Are bursts short (seconds) or sustained (minutes)?
01:47 Priya Raman: Usually 3-5 minute bursts during heavy usage, sometimes sustained for 15-20 minutes during demos.
01:55 Liam Chen: Ok, that's helpful. We typically characterize performance by request size and concurrency. For hosted, we have multi-tenant pools that get you fastest onboarding but less isolation; Dedicated gives predictable throughput per GPU and burst behavior; Private gives VPC and full control but needs provisioning.
02:14 Carlos Vega: Can you give a ballpark for tokens/sec and p95 per GPU? Like what can we realistically expect on dedicated?
02:21 Maya Singh: Ballpark numbers depend on model and quantization. For a 7B-ish transformer optimized with int8/4 quantization, you might see 200-600 tokens/sec sustained on a single A100/80GB equivalent with heavy batching. For p95 on short 150-token streaming requests at low concurrency, sub-200ms first-token is possible, completion p95 depends on tokens/sec and response length. For p95 <300-400ms for 150-token end-to-end, you'd need enough concurrency and lower queueing — that often means dedicated pools sized for your concurrency target.
03:07 Priya Raman: That 200-600 tokens/sec range is pretty wide. For our 150-token flows, what does that translate to p95 with concurrency 30?
03:15 Maya Singh: Rough calc: if a GPU sustained 500 tokens/sec, a 150-token response is ~0.3s generation time. Add overheads for routing and streaming — so 300-400ms is achievable, p95 threading in queueing could push it higher if you're overcommit. So to hit <300ms p95 at concurrency 30 we usually recommend dedicated capacity with autoscaling headroom or prefix KV caching for common prompts.
03:48 Dana Ortiz: Prefix KV cache — we've seen references. How intrusive is that to implement?
03:52 Maya Singh: It's mostly config on Redwood side; we can cache common prompts at routing layer, avoiding recompute of KV-cache for repeated prefixes. For your use-case with repeated enterprise intros or templates it often helps a lot.
04:05 Carlos Vega: Streaming is critical for UX. We need to ensure token-by-token latency is stable. Any constraints on streaming with Dedicated vs Hosted?
04:14 Liam Chen: Streaming works across all modes. Hosted has global optimizations and can be very fast, but if you need strict p95 SLOs and isolation, Dedicated gives you predictable per-GPU throughput and reserved capacity. Private adds network variability depending on your VPC setup.
04:30 Priya Raman: For benchmarking, what metrics should we capture? We want p50/p95/p99, tokens/sec, concurrency, time-to-first-token, and end-to-end completion time. Also GPU utilization and batching stats.
04:40 Maya Singh: Exactly. Our recommended benchmark plan will capture all those plus memory/KV-cache hit rates. We'll also run both streaming and non-streaming runs, and vary prompt lengths: short (50-200 tokens), medium (200-800), long (1k-2k).
04:56 Carlos Vega: Do you support auto-scaling for Dedicated? We might want to keep baseline 30 concurrency and auto-scale to 100 for peak.
05:03 Liam Chen: Yes — Dedicated supports autoscaling policies and burst capacity options. There's a tradeoff: reserved baseline gives lower unit cost, bursts are billed differently. We'll include cost/latency tradeoffs in the pricing sheet.
05:15 Dana Ortiz: On Private: network egress — if we host in our VPC, how does Redwood manage control plane and data plane? We need KMS keys held by us, audit logs forwarded to our SIEM, and minimal egress.
05:28 Maya Singh: For Private we support customer-managed KMS via HSM/KMS integrations, audit log exports, and a private control plane. Data plane can be placed in your VPC — you'll have routing control. We'll share the architecture doc.
05:39 Priya Raman: Competitors question — we've done some tests on Anthropic/Claude and OpenAI; we want to compare both latency & cost. How does Redwood compare in perf?
05:49 Liam Chen: Redwood's performance depends on the model variant. For open-models optimized with Redwood runtime we often get better throughput per GPU vs generic endpoints because of attention optimizations and kernel selection. We'll include a head-to-head benchmark plan; hard numbers will come from the pilot with your prompts.
06:05 Carlos Vega: Sounds good. What's a typical pilot size and timeline?
06:09 Maya Singh: Typical pilot: 1 week of bench runs + 1 week of analysis and follow-up. For you we'll propose a lightweight hosted run to start and then a dedicated/private run for apples-to-apples. We can start the week of 2026-04-06 if you can provide the prompt corpus.
06:26 Priya Raman: We can get that to you by 2026-04-01. We'll include traffic profile (concurrency histograms, token distribution).
06:33 Liam Chen: Great. Quick recap: we'll send Dedicated pricing and burst options, SOC2 and VPC architecture, and a benchmark plan. You'll send prompt set and traffic profile. Maya will run test scripts and we'll reconvene after pilot.
06:49 Carlos Vega: One more — GPU types. We prefer A100/80GB or newer. Any caveats?
06:54 Maya Singh: A100/80GB is supported and common for Dedicated; newer instances give more throughput. We'll note instance types and expected tokens/sec in the plan.
07:03 Dana Ortiz: Also SSO/SAML — we need enterprise SSO; can you support SCIM and role-based access?
07:09 Liam Chen: Yes, SSO, SCIM, RBAC are supported. We'll attach our security pack.
07:16 Carlos Vega: Perfect. That covers it for me.
07:18 Liam Chen: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with docs and schedule the pilot.
07:21 Meeting end.

Notes: transcript includes occasional mis-transcriptions (e.g., "K V cache" for KV cache), filler words, overlaps.
